UCI World Championships 2026 Women’s Elite Road Race: Our form guide

The women’s elite road race at the UCI World Championships takes place on Saturday, with 180.4km to decide who will wear the rainbow jersey in 2027.

After a steady start, the race takes eight laps of the same 13.4km hilly Montreal circuit as the men, with the Voie Camillien-Houde (1.7km, 7.7%) and Côte de Polytechnique (0.8km, 5.7%) ascents.

Last year, Canada’s Magdeleine Vallieres claimed a surprise victory in Rwanda ahead of Niamh Fisher-Black (New Zealand) and Mavi García (Spain), and she’ll be at home this year to try to defend her title, with Montreal just two hours away from where she grew up in Sherbrooke.

Demi Vollering (Netherlands)

European Road Race Champion Demi Vollering has won a lot throughout her career, but the World Championships rainbow bands elude her. This might just be the season that changes however, coming off another ferociously dominant year with two Grand Tours win and collection of Classics riders spend their whole careers chasing, and this punchy Montreal course suits her.

Her closest challenge came in the form of a silver medal in Glasgow in 2023. In 2024, she lost the sprint finish to come fifth, while in 2025 she won the sprint from the group of favourites but they lingered behind six others on the road. She’s unlikely to let a group get away again.

Kim Le Court-Pienaar (Mauritius)

Kim Le Court-Pienaar has made history pretty much every step of her career so far. In 2025 she became the first African rider to win a Monument at Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the first African rider to wear the yellow jersey at the Tour de France Femmes, and then also became the first to win a stage at the race too thanks to her Stage 5 victory.

The Mauritian Champion stormed to another victory at the Tour this year despite having a tough season with injury and also had a spirited GC fight, ending the race ninth overall. Just a few weeks later she carried that form into the Tour of Britain, where she picked up a maiden GC win.

Le Court-Pienaar has an excellent punch and a strong sprint finish, she should place highly here and has a really good chance at taking another famous victory.

Paula Blasi (Spain)

An Amstel Gold Race win. A podium at La Flèche Wallonne. Victory at La Vuelta Femenina. Fifth at the Tour de France Femmes. That’s just a snapshot of the incredible season Spain’s 23-year-old Paula Blasi has had so far. Barely more than a year into her pro career, Blasi been phenomenal to witness and could really do something on a hilly, attritional parcours at the World Championships.

In 2025, Blasi scored third place in the U23 road race, so this will be her elite level debut and she’s on co-leadership duties alongside UAE Team L’Imad teammate Mavi García, who finished third in last year’s race. This pairing could do something special.

Lotte Kopecky (Belgium)

Two-time World Champion Lotte Kopecky is utterly dominant at her best, crushing Classics and thriving in punishing conditions. However she hasn’t been at her best in the last two seasons, with her win rate showing just that, decreasing from 16 in 2024 (including the rainbow jersey) to just three as things stand in 2026.

Counting her out would be a dangerous move though. In 2023, she won the road race in a 5.6km solo attack, and in 2024 she won the small group sprint after a brilliant fighting performance and incredible support from Justine Ghekiere.

Noemi Rüegg (Switzerland)

It’s been a tough year for Noemi Rüegg, who fought back from injury sustained crashing out of the Vuelta while in the red jersey, but she scored multiple top tens over the opening three stages on home roads in Switzerland at the Tour de France Femmes. She loves hillys races and has one of the best kicks in the game. She has a strong team here with TT World Champion Marlen Reusser and could take inspiration from the success of EF Education-EasyPost teammate Magdeleine Vallieres last year.

Elisa Longo Borghini (Italy)

34-year-old Elisa Longo Borghini had a slow start to the season by her standards, missing out on a victory in the big Classics, but she achieved a huge third place at the Tour de France Femmes and still won stages across the UAE Tour, Giro d’Italia and Tour de Suisse. One look at her palmarès showcases her abilities in one-day races of all kinds over the years, whether it be the Tour of Flanders, Paris-Roubaix Femmes or Brabantse Pijl.

The multiple Italian national champion has never quite had the edge to secure higher than a bronze medal in the road race, coming third in 2020 and 2024. She did help the team to a gold medal in the mixed relay team time-trial at the World Championships last week though, and had an impressive showing in the individual time-trial to finish fourth.

Marlen Reusser (Switzerland)

Marlen Reusser has one gold medal from these World Championships already, claiming victory in the individual time-trial by some margin. The Swiss rider isn’t only fierce against the clock but it certainly helps her with solo attacks.

She’s had a strong season leading up to this, going late for final day and overall victory at the Tour de Suisse and having an excellent Tour de France until she crashed on the final stage. Her best result in the road race came in 2023 where she finished fourth, but has been strong in hilly Classics this year, beating Demi Vollering in the sprint to win Dwars door Vlaanderen in April.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Poland)

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney has had a season to remember, collecting a plethora of podiums in the Classics before coming so close to overall victory at the Tour after a commanding victory on Mont Ventoux. She hasn’t raced since the final stage of the Tour, so her form is somewhat of a mystery, but she always tends to show up in big races. Her best Worlds result to date is a bronze medal in 2021.

Others

24-year-old Puck Pieterse (Netherlands) has been flying. She won the mountains classification at the Tour de France Femmes after a Classics season in which she finished second at both Liège-Bastogne-Liège and La Flèche Wallonne and third at the Tour of Flanders. Franziska Koch (Germany) reigned victorious at Paris-Roubaix Femmes, doubled up in the National Championships and podiumed in the individual time-trial at the World Championships last week, it could be a step too far for her with the hills on offer, however nothing would be a surprise with the form she’s shown.

Keep an eye on Cédrine Kerbaol (France) too. She scored multiple top ten results across the Tour de France Femmes that resulted in sixth place overall and clocked fifth in the individual time-trial in Montreal.
